variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Feature engineering is the work of turning raw observations into model inputs that express a useful, reproducible signal. A feature can be a direct value, such as account age, or a derived value, such as purchases in the previous seven days.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “A useful feature must satisfy four invariants”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Available
pairs.detail: The value exists when the prediction is requested.
pairs.explanation: The value exists when the prediction is requested. Future events, delayed labels, and late-arriving records cannot silently enter historical training rows.

pairs.label: Reproducible
pairs.detail: Given the same entity, timestamp, raw inputs, and feature version, the offline and online paths produce the same value.
pairs.explanation: Given the same entity, timestamp, raw inputs, and feature version, the offline and online paths produce the same value.

pairs.label: Useful
pairs.detail: The feature improves an appropriate holdout metric or important slice enough to justify its complexity and cost.
pairs.explanation: The feature improves an appropriate holdout metric or important slice enough to justify its complexity and cost.

pairs.label: Operable
pairs.detail: The feature has a type, owner, source, freshness target, null policy, lineage, monitoring plan, and safe fallback.
pairs.explanation: The feature has a type, owner, source, freshness target, null policy, lineage, monitoring plan, and safe fallback.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. Read ML Fundamentals first if prediction units, labels, training splits, and generalization are unfamiliar.

variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Select features by evidence and total cost”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Filter methods
pairs.detail: Rank inputs using statistics independent of the final model.
pairs.explanation: Rank inputs using statistics independent of the final model. They are inexpensive, but they can miss interactions and do not prove production value.

pairs.label: Wrapper methods
pairs.detail: Train repeated candidate subsets against the chosen metric.
pairs.explanation: Train repeated candidate subsets against the chosen metric. They capture model-specific interactions but can be computationally expensive and unstable on small data.

pairs.label: Embedded methods
pairs.detail: Use regularization, tree splits, or learned gates to reduce effective inputs while training.
pairs.explanation: Use regularization, tree splits, or learned gates to reduce effective inputs while training. Validate stability across folds and time periods.

variants.prompt: A fraud label arrives 30 days after a transaction. Can that label be a feature for the original transaction-time prediction?
options: No, it was unavailable at prediction time and would leak the outcome
Yes, because it is eventually stored
Yes, if the model is tree-based
Only when the label is standardized
variants.explanation: Feature eligibility is defined at prediction time. A later outcome may be the training label, but it cannot be an input to that earlier prediction.
